criteria.note: The TL;DR and the 'If You're Celiac, Start Here' block deliver the trip-planning answer (what's unsafe, three dedicated venues, the allergy phrase, store baseline) inside the first ~200 words, with the NCGS caveat stated up front rather than buried.
Title is 35 chars plus the 20-char site suffix (55 total), description is 146 chars, keyword present in both, and the shared words are keyword usage rather than repeated phrasing.

Headings are argumentative rather than labelling ('What Korean Food Actually Looks Like, From a Gluten Angle', 'The One Phrase That Actually Works', 'Reading Korean Labels: Four Words That Matter'), and a heading-only skim reconstructs the whole method.
Six distinct in-body links (restaurants, bakeries, phrases, BBQ, labels, snacks) each sit where a reader would want the deeper dive, plus /about in the contact context.

All five frontmatter Q/As are reproduced verbatim as visible content, each stands alone as a rich result, and the substance (tamari, three Tier 1 venues, 10% wheat bakery, allergen realities) is carried by the body.

Dense first-hand specifics: the summer-2025 franchise call, the bakery owner's '90% rice flour, 10% wheat flour' answer, the pink-vs-green Chamsal Seolbyeong packets, the online loaf quietly renamed, named dishes ordered at each venue.
Korean terms romanised (ganjang, milgaru, ppeongttwigi), named products (Goraesa, Poca Chip Original vs Onion, Chamsal Seolbyeong), and checkable figures (19-item declaration list, 10% wheat ratio).

Primary sources are linked with retrieval or publication dates — the MFDS 식품등의 표시기준 with an 'as of August 2026' framing, Orion's own product page 'retrieved August 2026', and the blogger roundup 'published October 2023'.
The piece states repeatedly what its NCGS-standard method cannot establish, retracts an unverifiable GFCO claim, ages its own franchise call, and carries no affiliate or undisclosed commercial links.

findings.quote: Ask for unseasoned meat ("양념 안 한 고기 있나요?"), bring GF soy sauce, and skip sauced banchan sides.
findings.why: This is the one FAQ whose operational detail (the unseasoned-meat phrase, fresh grill plate, clean tongs) appears nowhere in the body outside the FAQ block itself, so the rich-result answer is thinner on page support than the other four.
findings.fix: Add one or two sentences in the phrase section giving 양념 안 한 고기 있나요? with romanisation and the grill-plate/tongs request, so the BBQ FAQ is corroborated by body copy as well as by the FAQ block.

findings.fix: Render only the links to live posts and hold the rest until publication, or mark unpublished entries as plain text without an href.

findings.fix: Add a short line per Tier 1 venue recording what the kitchen said about dedicated equipment and flour handling, dated — that converts the celiac framing from disclaimer into evidence.

criteria.note: Safety-critical claims (labelling law, allergen count, snack allergens, franchise call) are sourced and dated, but several food-composition claims are stated as fact without a source or an explicit observation marker.

Product names, dates and figures are checkable and mutually consistent, but the FAQ frames a Pyeongtaek café as an answer to a Seoul question, and one cited URL carries mismatched internal identifiers.
criteria.evidence_quote:
**Is any restaurant in Seoul truly dedicated gluten-free?**
Yes, but few. 237 Pizza (Hannam), monil2 house (Yeonnam), and Cafe Rebirth (Pyeongtaek) are the three we trust most.

criteria.note: The piece states how it knows (visits, a dated phone call, label reading, a cited blogger roundup) and what each method cannot establish, including retracting an unverifiable certification claim.

No absolute safety guarantees, cross-contamination handled at grill, kitchen and packaging level, and celiac risk is consistently escalated above the author's NCGS baseline rather than merged with it.
Retrieval dates are given, the 2023 blogger source and the 2025 franchise call have their elapsed time stated, and reformulation risk is flagged as a standing caution.
Korean terms, phrases and product categories are rendered correctly, and the mandatory-allergen scope (wheat yes, barley and rye no) is stated accurately and given operational consequences.
The reader gets the exact Korean strings to scan, a primary-law link, a manufacturer product page, and scripts to re-confirm with staff and at their own branch.

findings.quote:
**Is any restaurant in Seoul truly dedicated gluten-free?**
Yes, but few. 237 Pizza (Hannam), monil2 house (Yeonnam), and Cafe Rebirth (Pyeongtaek) are the three we trust most.
findings.why: The question scopes to Seoul; Cafe Rebirth is described elsewhere in the body as 'about an hour south of Seoul' in Gyeonggi. The parenthetical keeps a reader from being actively misled, but a traveller scanning the FAQ could plan a Seoul day around a place that is a round trip out of the city.
findings.fix: Reword the FAQ answer to 'Two in Seoul — 237 Pizza (Hannam) and monil2 house (Yeonnam) — plus Cafe Rebirth, about an hour south in Pyeongtaek.'

findings.why: The path segment (view/27) and the query parameter (goodsno=26) disagree, which is the signature of a hand-assembled rather than copied URL. On a page where the citation is doing the work of a safety claim about a specific chip flavour, a link that resolves to the wrong product silently removes the reader's ability to check.
findings.fix: Re-open the link, confirm it lands on the Poca Chip Original allergen table, and replace it with the canonical URL; note the retrieval date beside it as you already do elsewhere.

findings.why: Stated as a bare fact with no source and no observation marker. Traditional doenjang is soybeans, salt and water; wheat appears in some commercial formulations. The claim errs toward avoidance so it is not a safety hazard, but it is the kind of compositional assertion a reader will repeat to a kitchen.
findings.fix: Narrow to commercial product and attach evidence, e.g. 'Commercial doenjang sometimes lists wheat (밀) — check 원재료명 on the tub,' with one manufacturer label cited.

findings.quote: Safe baseline is eggs, fruit, plain yogurt, a few confirmed chips.
findings.why: The TL;DR calls the chips 'confirmed', but the body downgrades most of that list to 'leads' traced to a 2023 blogger roundup, with only the Orion entries manufacturer-sourced. A reader who acts on the summary alone inherits a confidence the body withdraws.
findings.fix: Change to 'a couple of chips we have manufacturer-label evidence for — see the store section for which, and re-check the packet.'
